The question for tonight

When an AI system works in testing and fails in real use, what usually went wrong?

The technology

The model is not good enough at the job.

The data

Real-use data looks different from the data it learned on.

The people

The tool does not fit how people actually do the work.

Write down your guess. Each case tonight ends by sorting itself into one of these three.

Part 1

Four Domains, Five Cases

Each case shows a different way a working model can fail, or succeed, once it meets real people.

Healthcare × 2FinanceDefenseEducation
Part 1 · Case 1 · Healthcare

Eye screening in Thailand

You will learn
  • The three stages every AI system passes: lab test, pilot, deployment
  • Why accuracy alone hides the patients a system turned away
Guide Part 1, the eye clinic (Beede et al., 2020; Heaven, 2020).
The case · Thailand · 2018 to 2019

Thailand had too few eye doctors to catch diabetic blindness.

  • Diabetes damages the back of the eye.Caught early, it can be treated. Caught late, it causes blindness.
  • 4.5 million patients. About 200 specialists.More than 20,000 patients for every specialist. Results took up to 10 weeks.
  • Google Health built a model that read the photos.Over 90 percent accurate in testing, with a result in under 10 minutes.
  • It was built to reject blurry or dark photos.A quality cutoff, so it would never answer from a bad photo. With Thailand's Ministry of Public Health, it went into 11 clinics in Pathum Thani and Chiang Mai.
Ask: "If you were Google, what would you build?" Most say: something to read the photos. That was a good idea. Nothing that follows is about a bad idea.
Predict before you see it

Out of every 100 clinic photos, how many did the system reject as too poor to read?

5%
your guess
vs.
more than 20
rejected in the clinics

Those patients were sent to another clinic on another day. The "90 percent accurate" number never counted them.

Most guess under 10. The answer is more than 1 in 5. Ask: "Who paid for the rejected photos?" The patient.
Key terms · Case 1

Every AI system passes through three stages.

Lab test
Scoring a model on saved data. Nobody uses it for real work yet.
Example Google's 90 percent, measured on saved photos.
Never tests real people, rooms, or workload.
Pilot
A small, short trial with real users and extra help.
Example Two clinics for three months, researchers on site.
Never tests life without volunteers and helpers.
Deployment
Everyday use. The extra help is gone, and decisions depend on it.
Example Every clinic, every day.
Never tests nothing. This is the real test.

Each stage tests something the stage before it never tested. Problems show up when things get real and help goes away.

Key terms · Case 1

Accuracy only counts the cases where the system gave an answer.

Accuracy
Of the cases a system answered, the share it got right.
right ÷ (right + wrong)
Eye clinic 71 ÷ 79 = 90%
Answer rate
Of all cases, the share the system gave any answer for. Also called coverage.
(right + wrong) ÷ all
Eye clinic 79 ÷ 100 = 79%

Ask both numbers. Then ask the real one: out of everyone who walked in, how many left with a correct result?

Worked example

Watch 100 patients turn into 71 correct results.

100 patients walk in

What the vendor reports

71 of 100
Try it

Three companies sell you an eye scanner. Which would you buy?

Cases with no answer Accuracy when it answers
Accuracy
Answer rate
Right out of 100

RightFalse alarmMissNo answer
7 of 100 patients have the disease. A: answers everyone, 4 sick patients told they are fine. B: rejects 30, 95 percent on the rest, about 67 helped. C: says "no disease" to all, 93 percent accurate, misses all 7.
Simulation · The eye clinic

Same model, three stages. Then you fix the clinic.

Room lighting Patients per hour Upload wait per photo Quality cutoff
Step 1: run Lab test, Pilot, Deployment. Step 2: from Deployment, get fewer than 5 patients a day with no result, keeping accuracy at 90 percent or more.
CorrectWrongSent awayNot seen
The fix: lighting near 80 plus background upload. Lowering the cutoff alone drops accuracy below 90.
What happened

The model never changed. The clinic did.

  • Dim rooms made worse photos.The model learned on bright, sharp scans, so more clinic photos got rejected.
  • Slow internet made the nurse wait.One nurse in the study screened only 10 patients in two hours.
  • Lowering the cutoff trades rejections for wrong answers.Fixing the room helped without adding errors.
Main causeDataSecond causePeople and workflow

2. Google's "over 90 percent accurate" came from which stage?

Your capstone · Case 1

Where would your system meet its own "dark clinic"?

Auto repair garage

Lab: trained on clean repair manuals.
Real use: mechanics type "makes a weird noise when cold."

Aircraft maintenance

Lab: damage photos from a bright hangar.
Real use: flight line photos at dusk, in rain.

Berry farm

Real use: phone photos of muddy rows in full sun.

Ask yourself: what will real-use data look like at my organization, and what will my system do when it cannot give an answer?
Part 1 · Case 2 · Healthcare

The sepsis alert

You will learn
  • The two kinds of wrong answer, and why they do not cost the same
  • Why mostly-wrong alerts make people stop looking
Guide Part 1, the sepsis alert (Wong et al., 2021).
The case · Michigan Medicine · 2018 to 2019

Hundreds of hospitals turned on a sepsis alert that no outside group had tested.

  • Sepsis is the body's extreme reaction to an infection.About 1 in 3 patients who die in a hospital has sepsis. Treating it early saves lives.
  • Epic sells the health-records software used by 56 percent of U.S. hospitals.Its software includes a sepsis alert, the Epic Sepsis Model. Hundreds of hospitals switched it on.
  • Its accuracy numbers came from Epic's own documents.No independent test had been published, even though hospitals relied on it every day.
  • Michigan Medicine tested it on its own patients.38,455 hospital stays, December 2018 to October 2019. You will see what they found after the simulation.
Sources: Wong et al. (2021), JAMA Internal Medicine; Michigan Medicine news release. The 56 percent figure is Epic's share of U.S. hospitals and health systems, quoted by the Michigan team. Ask: "If your hospital bought this, how would you know it worked?" Most students will say "the vendor told us." That is the point of the case.
Key terms · Case 2

A system can be wrong in two different ways.

False alarm
The system flags something that is fine.
Example An alert on a healthy patient.
Miss
The system says "fine" about something that is not.
Example No alert on a patient with sepsis.
Sensitivity
Of the real cases, the share the system catches.
Example Catches 1 of 3 sepsis patients: 33%.
Alert fatigue
People stop paying attention because most alerts are wrong.
Example A nurse dismisses an alert that is usually false.

A miss and a false alarm both count as "wrong." In a hospital, a miss can kill. A false alarm wastes a nurse's time.

The simulation

You are the night nurse. 40 beds, 12 hours, 6 checks.

  • Sepsis is an infection that turns deadly fast.Signs: heart rate over 100 and temperature of 38° or higher.
  • An alert flashes when its score says a patient may have sepsis.When it fires, you check that patient or dismiss the alert.
  • You only have time for 6 checks.Looking at a bed's numbers is free. A check confirms sepsis and starts care.
Simulation · The night shift
Hour 0 of 12 Checks left 6 Sepsis caught 0 of 3
Alert firing♥ 97 · 37.8° early warning♥ 112 · 38.4° sepsis signsCare started
The 6 false alerts all have normal vitals. Bed 19 turns amber at hour 4; bed 12 at hour 7 (alert only at 10); bed 36 at hour 8, never alerted. Ask: "When the alert and the numbers disagreed, which did you trust?"
The real case · University of Michigan (2021)

The vendor said the alert was good. The hospital tested it on its own patients.

External validation
Someone other than the builder tests the model on data the builder never saw.
Michigan's score
0.63

The vendor said 0.76 to 0.83.

Patients flagged
18%

Your shift: 7 of 40

Alerts that were real
12%

Your shift: 1 of 7

Sepsis cases missed
67%

Your shift: 2 of 3

Scores are AUC: how often the model ranks a sick patient above a healthy one. 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. Wong et al. (2021), 38,455 hospital stays.

What happened

A bad alert is worse than no alert, because people stop looking.

  • It learned what doctors had already noticed.The vendor trained it to predict when a doctor would write "sepsis." That does not help the doctor.
  • Michigan graded it more strictly.No credit for alerts that fired after the staff had already acted.
  • Wrong alarms taught people to ignore alarms.And patients with no alert got checked less, because nurses expected a warning.
Main causeData and definitionsSecond causePeople (alert fatigue)
Check yourself · Case 2

Two quick questions.

1. Your alert caught 1 of the 3 sepsis patients. What is its sensitivity?

2. A hospital tests a vendor's model on its own patients before turning it on. What is that called?

Your capstone · Case 2

If your system raises alerts, how many will be false?

Security operations center

Analysts get thousands of alerts a day, most harmless. Alert fatigue is the biggest problem in the field.

Firmware security

A scanner that flags every odd line of code buries the one real weakness.

Auto repair garage

A tool that says "check the transmission" on every car teaches mechanics to ignore it.

Ask yourself: for my system, which costs more, a miss or a false alarm? Who pays each one?
Part 1 · Case 3 · Finance

Zillow Offers

You will learn
  • What stakes are, and why the same model can be safe in one job and costly in another
  • Why a changing world breaks a model trained on the past
Guide Part 1, Zillow Offers (Zillow Group, 2021).
The case · Zillow · 2018 to 2021

Zillow bet that its pricing model could buy houses, not just price them.

  • Zillow is a real estate website that shows a value estimate for millions of homes.The estimate, called the Zestimate, has run on the site since 2006.
  • In 2018, Zillow launched Zillow Offers.It bought homes straight from owners at a price based on its model, fixed them up, and resold them.
  • The business grew fast.In one three-month period of 2021, Zillow bought 9,680 homes.
  • The plan depended on one thing: the model's price had to be close to what each house would really sell for.The simulation shows what happens when it is not.
Sources: Zillow Group Form 10-Q for Q3 2021; CNN Business, November 2, 2021. "iBuying" is the industry name for this business model. Ask: "On the website, who pays when the estimate is wrong? When Zillow buys the house?"
Key terms · Case 3

Same model, same errors. Only the cost of an error changed.

Stakes
What a wrong answer costs, and who pays for it.
Low a wrong home-value estimate on a website costs Zillow $0.
High buying a house at a wrong price loses real money.
Winner's curse
When you only win the deals you overpaid for, because sellers turn down your low offers.
Example Every house Zillow bought was one its model had overpriced.

Job 1 (since 2006): show an estimate

Wrong estimate: costs Zillow $0.

Job 2 (from 2018): buy the house

Wrong estimate: Zillow loses money.

Simulation · The home-buying desk
Step 2 shows the winner's curse. Step 3: 2 to 3 percent margin earns most. Step 4: same margin loses millions when prices fall.
What happened

Zillow's model didn't get worse. Its job got harder.

  • The winner's curse.Sellers took the high offers and refused the low ones.
  • The market turned. The model kept predicting higher prices.It learned from years of rising prices. Zillow owned houses worth less than it paid.
  • Zillow stopped. That was the right call.November 2021: closed the business, wrote down about $304 million, cut about 25 percent of staff.
Main causeTechnologyWhyThe job became predicting future prices
Check yourself · Case 3

Two quick questions.

1. Zillow used the same pricing model for its website and for buying homes. What changed?

2. Which of these is a sound recommendation when a model's mistakes cost too much?

Discussion · Case 3 · Your capstone

Is your system giving advice, or making the decision?

SuggestsA person checksActs on its own
Think tank suggest a topic label → decide who is cleared to read it
Trucking pre-fill a form for a clerk → file customs papers alone
Aircraft point an inspector to a spot → clear the aircraft to fly
1Think · 1 min

Which one is your system: it suggests, a person checks its answer, or it acts on its own? Write it down.

2Pair · 2 min

Tell a partner: if it is wrong, who pays, and how much?

3Share

Would that cost change if no person checked its answer?

Run it as think, pair, share. One minute alone, two minutes with a partner, then use Pick a student for two or three answers. Push for a number or a concrete cost: a fine, a grounded aircraft, a customer lost. Then ask the follow-up: if the system moved one step right on the line, what would have to be true first? Ties back to Zillow: the same model went from "suggests" (website estimate) to "acts on its own" (buying houses), and the cost of a wrong answer jumped.
Part 1 · Case 4 · Defense

Predictive maintenance

You will learn
  • Why an accurate forecast can still prevent nothing
  • What an organization needs before it can act on a model's output
Guide Part 1, predictive maintenance (GAO, 2022).
The case · U.S. Department of Defense · 2002 to 2022

The military has tried to predict breakdowns for 20 years. Auditors checked how it went.

  • A vehicle that breaks without warning is out of service, and the unit is less ready.Predictive maintenance uses sensors, data, and AI to fix parts when the evidence says they need it.
  • The Department of Defense first made it policy in 2002.In 2020, it named this approach a primary strategy for maintaining its equipment.
  • In 2022, two audits checked progress.The Inspector General found no service had fully put it in place. The Government Accountability Office (GAO) visited units and interviewed maintenance officials.
  • GAO made 16 recommendations to the Army, Marine Corps, Navy, and Air Force.They asked for plans to put predictive maintenance in place and a way to measure whether it works.
Sources: GAO-23-105556 (December 2022), "Military Readiness: Actions Needed to Further Implement Predictive Maintenance on Weapon Systems"; DoD Inspector General report DODIG-2022-103 (June 2022); DoD Instruction 4151.22 (August 2020). Many students have worked in maintenance. Ask: "Would your shop have acted on a forecast that said a part would fail in three weeks?"
Key term · Case 4

Fix it before it breaks, if anyone is allowed to.

Predictive maintenance
Fixing equipment when sensor data shows it is wearing out, not on a fixed schedule.
Example A model warns three weeks before a part fails. Fix early: 1 day out of service. Let it break: 10 days.

The idea is simple. Getting an organization to act on the forecast is the hard part.

Simulation · The motor pool
Your question: the forecast is 85 percent accurate. What does the motor pool need so it actually prevents breakdowns?

RunningForecast: will failFixed earlyBroke down
Run the year with nothing checked first.
Nothing checked: 5 prevented. Better model: still 5. Permission + parts: 8. + trust: 12. All four: 18 of 19.
What happened

A better model changed nothing. Changing the organization changed everything.

  • The forecast alone prevented almost nothing.Even at 99 percent accuracy, warnings sat unread.
  • Each change needed the others.Permission with no parts: nothing to install. Parts with no trust: the part sits on the shelf.
  • Auditors made 16 recommendations.Every one was about organizing, planning, or measuring. Not one asked for a better model.
Main causePeople and how they work
Check yourself · Case 4

Two quick questions.

1. Your commander asks for a more accurate forecast. Based on the motor pool, what do you say?

2. Replacing a part because sensor data shows wear is called…

Your capstone · Case 4

Who has to act on your system's output, and are they set up to?

Aircraft maintenance

The model flags damage. Does the inspector have authority to ground the aircraft?

Hospital system

The model predicts who will get worse. Who owns it after the pilot ends?

Berry farm

The model spots disease early. Are supplies and workers ready that week?

Ask yourself: which of permission, parts, trust, or an owner is missing at my organization?
Part 1 · Case 5 · Education

Pounce at Georgia State

You will learn
  • What a tool built for one domain looks like
  • Why the simplest tool in the Guide worked best
Guide Part 1, Pounce (Page and Gehlbach, 2017).
The case · Georgia State University, Atlanta · Summer 2016

Students who said yes to college were not showing up in the fall.

  • Georgia State is a large public university in Atlanta.Many students are from low-income families or are first in their family to attend college.
  • Between "yes" and the first day, students must finish about five tasks.Financial aid, final transcript, shots record, loan forms, orientation. Miss one and you cannot enroll.
  • Every year, 10 to 20 percent of college-bound students never arrive.Higher for low-income and first-generation students, who often have no one to ask over the summer.
  • The problem was paperwork, not ability.Georgia State asked: could an AI texting assistant answer students' questions at any hour?
Source: Page and Gehlbach (2017), AERA Open. The 10 to 20 percent national range is from that paper. Ask: "Who here had a form go missing before your first semester? Who did you call?" Many military-connected students will have a story.
Key terms · Case 5

Three terms you need for this case.

Summer melt
Students who are accepted and plan to attend college, but never enroll in the fall.
Example A student pays the deposit in May, misses the loan form in July, and never starts.
AI texting assistant
A chatbot that answers questions by text message, using answers its builders loaded into it.
Example "When is orientation?" gets an answer at 11 PM, no office needed.
Randomized trial
Split people by chance into two groups. One gets the tool, one does not. Compare the results.
Example Half the incoming students got Pounce. Half did not.

The randomized trial is how Georgia State knew Pounce caused the change. Without the comparison group, a good year could look like success.

Connect "randomized trial" to Mayo Clinic in Part 2, which used the same method. Quick check: "If Georgia State had given Pounce to everyone, how would they know it worked?" They could not tell it apart from a good year.
The case · What they built and what happened

Pounce cut summer melt by 21 percent.

  • Georgia State built Pounce with AdmitHub, an education technology company.It texted students over the summer and answered their questions at any hour.
  • It was connected to the university's own student records.It knew which tasks each student had left, so it only sent reminders that applied to them.
  • Half the incoming students got Pounce. Half did not.Students who had Pounce were more likely to finish their tasks and enroll on time.
  • Summer melt dropped 21 percent.It helped students who had already decided to come. For undecided students, it did almost nothing.
Source: Page and Gehlbach (2017). Connecting Pounce to the student records was new for summer melt programs; earlier efforts sent the same message to everyone, and students tuned them out. Next: the simulation lets students test which design choices made the difference.
Simulation · The summer assistant
Your question: which design choices make the assistant actually help? Run it off first, then add one choice at a time.
Students:
No-shows
–
Turned off texts
–
To counselors
–
Share of questions the assistant answeredQuestions sent to counselors
Run the summer with the assistant off first.
What happened

Pounce worked because every choice fit this one school.

  • It used the school's own records.No nagging about finished forms, so students kept the texts on.
  • It gave this school's answers.Counselors wrote the first 250. The knowledge base grew past 1,000.
  • A real counselor stood behind it.Only 13.5 percent of students ever needed one.
  • It measured what mattered: enrollment.And it cost $7 to $15 per student, against $100 to $200 for counselors alone.
Why it workedLocal dataPeople in the loopOne clear job
Check yourself · Case 5

2. Pounce barely helped undecided students. What does that teach?

Your capstone · Case 5

Build it for your organization, not for "any organization."

Auto repair garage

Own data: this shop's repair records, not a general chatbot.
Hard cases: the senior mechanic.

Think tank

Own data: this office's own categories.
Hard cases: an analyst decides.

Trucking company

If paperwork follows fixed rules, ordinary software may beat AI. Know when not to use AI.

Ask yourself: what data does only my organization have, and who handles what my system cannot?

Part 2

Fitting a Solution to Its Domain

Part 1 showed what happened. Part 2 explains why, in seven ideas, and ends with a method you can use on any AI system.

Part 2 · Section 1

Domain shift and shortcuts

You will learn
  • The four ways a new place can differ from the place a model learned
  • How a model can score high by learning the wrong thing
  • Tonight you train a real neural network and watch it happen
Guide Part 2, section 1 (Zech et al., 2018).
Key terms · Section 1

A score describes only the data it was tested on.

Domain
The area of work where a system is used: its data, people, equipment, and rules.
Example A Thai eye clinic. A Michigan hospital.
Domain shift
Real-use data differs from the training data in a way that matters, so results drop.
Example Learned on sharp photos, met dim ones.
Shortcut
A pattern that raises a model's score but has nothing to do with the task.
Example Recognizing which hospital took the X-ray.
Four ways a new place can differ from where the model learned

Before you use a model somewhere new, check these four differences.

Equipment

Different camera, scanner, sensor, lighting, or network.

You saw it

Eye clinic; X-rays

Population

Different patients, customers, students, or vehicles.

You saw it

Sepsis alert at Michigan

Definitions

The same word is recorded differently in two places.

You saw it

What counts as sepsis

Time

The world changes after the model is trained.

You saw it

Zillow in 2021

The only defense: test on data from the place where the tool will be used, before anyone depends on it.

Part 2 · Section 2

Why AI projects fail

You will learn
  • RAND's five root causes of AI project failure
  • Which one is most common, and how to spot it early
Guide Part 2, section 2 (Ryseff et al., 2024).
RAND (2024) · interviews with 65 experienced builders

Five root causes of AI project failure, most common first.

Root cause
The underlying reason something failed, not the first symptom you notice.
1
Leaders misunderstand the problem.The model gets tuned to the wrong goal. Eye clinic: accuracy, not patients helped.
2
The right data isn't there.Not enough, or not the right kind. No dim clinic photos in training.
3
Technology comes first.Pick the shiny tool, then hunt for a problem. Pounce did the opposite.
4
The basics around the model are weak.No reliable way to move data, run the model, or watch it. Clinic uploads; motor pool parts.
5
The problem is too hard.Beyond what AI can do reliably. Predicting a falling housing market.

84 percent of industry interviewees named a leadership failure. Most interviewees were engineers, which RAND says may tilt the blame toward leaders.

Check yourself · Section 2

Name the root cause.

1. A manager says, "We need a GenAI chatbot. Find something for it to do." Which root cause is this?

2. A team builds a model that is very accurate, but the goal was "screen more patients," and it screens fewer. Which root cause?

Part 2 · Section 3

Domain knowledge belongs in the design

You will learn
  • The five things a domain's experts know that builders cannot guess
  • Why that knowledge has to arrive before the tool does
Key term · Section 3

Every case that went wrong was missing something only insiders knew.

Domain knowledge
A domain is an area of work or study: the profession you are training for, such as healthcare, logistics, or cybersecurity. Domain knowledge is what people who work in a domain know that outsiders don't: what words mean, which data to trust, and how the work really gets done.
The expert suppliesWhy builders can't guess itWhere you saw it
What the words meanThe same label is recorded differently from place to place.Sepsis: two definitions, two scores
Which data to trustSome fields are typed in by people with no reason to be careful.RAND's interviewees
How the work gets doneThe pace and equipment are only visible on site.Eye clinic: lighting and uploads
What success isThe score that matters is rarely the model's accuracy.Pounce: enrollment
What is allowedLaws and policies decide who may act on an output.Motor pool: replacing a part early
About one in five industry engineers RAND interviewed said a lack of domain understanding had caused projects to fail. Experts sometimes hold back because they think the tool will replace them; a project has to give them a reason to share.
Check yourself · Section 3

Who should have been in the room?

1. A team builds a model to predict which soldiers will miss a training deadline. Nobody on the team has served. Who could have told them what they'd get wrong?

2. How did Pounce build domain knowledge in?

Part 2 · Section 4

The Fit Check

You will learn
  • Five questions to ask before a tool moves to a new place
  • How to use them to recommend adopt, adapt, or stop
Key term · Section 4

Before the five questions, ask one more: is this a job for AI at all?

Fit Check
Five questions to ask before a tool moves into a new domain.

Data

Does the data here look like what it learned from?

Users

Who acts on it, and what do they do when it's wrong?

Workflow

Where does it fit in the day? What happens with no answer?

Stakes

What does a miss cost? A false alarm? Who pays?

Rules

Which laws and approvals apply? Who answers for it?

Higher stakes raise the testing bar. A movie recommender can learn from its mistakes in public. A medical alert has to prove itself first.

Simulation · Run the Fit Check

A U.S. city's chatbot is moving to a base housing office in Japan.

The city's GenAI chatbot answers questions about trash, parking, repairs, and permits. For each clue, tap the Fit Check question it raises and the best way to adapt. (Invented scenario.)

A sample recommendation

Our call: adapt it. Don't switch it on as-is.

  • Data: almost every clue showed a difference from the city.Japanese trash rules, residents whose first language isn't English, a score measured on city questions.
  • Start small, with local answers.General housing questions only. Test on 100 real resident questions first.
  • Stakes: people handle repairs, leases, and safety.Same-day work orders for gas, mold, and broken heat.
  • Rules: nothing goes live until data storage is approved.Conversations are stored on U.S. servers.
Part 2 · Section 5

Five ways to adapt a tool

You will learn
  • Five fixes for the problems the Fit Check finds
  • Why "stop" is always a sound answer
Section 5

Each fix answers a Fit Check problem.

1Narrow the jobOne task, one measure of success.Pounce: paperwork only
2Use local dataRetrain on this organization's data, or at least test on it.Your neural network, step 3
3Move the cutoffMatch it to what mistakes cost here.Zillow's safety margin
4Change the workflowWho sees the output, when, and what they do next.Background uploads at the clinic
5Send hard cases to a personAnd feed their answers back into the tool.Pounce's counselors
✕StopIf the job is too hard or a mistake costs too much.Zillow, 2021

The same moves work for GenAI tools: narrow the prompt's job, give it your organization's documents, and have a person check what matters.

Part 2 · Section 6

Five strategies that carry across domains

You will learn
  • The five habits every success in this unit shared
  • How to build them into your capstone plan
Section 6

What carries from one domain to the next.

  1. Phase it in.Pilot first, measure, then widen. Mayo ran a trial before routine use.
  2. Keep people in the loop.The tool recommends; a person decides. Pounce's counselors.
  3. Build a feedback loop.Every correction makes the tool better. Pounce grew from 250 to 1,000+ answers.
  4. Make it explainable.Users must see why it flagged something, or they ignore it. The sepsis alert.
  5. Mix the team.Builders plus people who work in the domain. BMW's line workers labeled the photos.

What carries across domains: the technique and the method. What has to be redone in every domain: the data, the cutoff, the workflow, and the rules.

Part 2 · Section 7

Two cases that worked

You will learn
  • How Mayo Clinic proved an AI tool in everyday care
  • How BMW put its own workers in charge of the training data
Healthcare · Mayo Clinic (2021)

An AI reading of a routine heart test found disease doctors were missing.

  • The model reads an ECG, a fast and cheap heart test.It flags a weak heart pump (low ejection fraction) that usually needs a costly scan to find.
  • It was tested in routine care, not just in a lab.348 primary care clinicians in 120 care teams at 45 sites were randomly split. Only one group saw the AI result.
  • Diagnoses rose 32 percent.About 5 new diagnoses for every 1,000 patients screened. Doctors still decided whether to order the scan.
StrategiesPhased in with a trialDoctor decidesTested in real use
EAGLE trial, Mayo Clinic (2021); model from Attia et al. (2019). The trial also studied the top users and non-users to learn how to improve adoption: a feedback loop.
Manufacturing · BMW Group (2019)

BMW's line workers built the AI that checks their own work.

  • A camera checks each finished car against its order.For example, is the right model badge on the car? AI compares the live image with the order data.
  • Workers take the photos and mark the defects.About 100 images per feature: perfect parts, parts with dust, parts with oil. That stopped dust from being mistaken for cracks.
  • Simple, narrow jobs on purpose.A mobile standard camera. No advanced IT skills needed. "We rely entirely on the experience and expertise of our employees."
StrategiesMixed teamLocal dataNarrow job
BMW Group press release, July 15, 2019. In use in series production since 2018.

2. Why did BMW's system learn to tell dust from cracks?

GenAI gives a first draft. Check every line against what you know about your organization, then write your own answer. Cite GenAI if you use its words.

In the hosted version, this calls GenAI directly. On GitHub Pages, it opens Claude or ChatGPT with the prompt filled in. Ask: "What did it get wrong about your organization?" That is domain knowledge GenAI doesn't have.

Your capstone · Week 6: The Real Case

Answer these five about your own system.

  1. Where did my data come from, and where will it be used?Name one difference: equipment, population, definitions, or time.
  2. The Fit Check: one sentence each.Data, users, workflow, stakes, rules.
  3. Which fix does my system need most?Narrow it, local data, cutoff, workflow, or a person.
  4. Who owns it after the pilot?How will they know if it stops working?
  5. What result would make me say "stop"?The hardest one, and the most important.
Back to the question

When AI fails in real use, what usually went wrong?

Technology

Once: Zillow, after the job got harder.

Data

The eye clinic, the sepsis alert, your neural network.

People

Predictive maintenance. Second cause at the clinic and the hospital.

Mostly the data and the people, not the model. The success story, Pounce, built its domain in from day one.

Unit 6 terms

Every term from tonight, in one place.

Lab test scoring on saved data
Pilot small trial with extra help
Deployment everyday use, no extra help
Accuracy right, of the cases answered
Answer rate share given any answer
False alarm flags something fine
Miss says "fine" when it is not
Sensitivity share of real cases caught
Alert fatigue ignoring mostly-wrong alerts
External validation tested by others on new data
Stakes what an error costs, who pays
Predictive maintenance fix when data shows wear
Domain the area of work a system serves
Domain shift new data differs, results drop
Shortcut score boost unrelated to the task
Root cause the underlying reason it failed
Domain knowledge what insiders know
Fit Check data, users, workflow, stakes, rules
